question: A viewer watches you make soup and asks, “Could you talk us through it?” What does she want?
choices: A chance to talk to the other viewers.
A shorter version with the sound off.
An explanation as you show each step.
A list of other soups she might like.
note: “Talk us through it” asks how you do something, step by step. A list of dishes would answer “What else could I make?”

picture.alt: A cooking pot and wooden spoon.

question: “The clip is good. I’d cut out the long wait for the bus.” What change does your partner suggest?
choices: Move that part to the beginning.
Record that part from closer up.
Describe that part in more detail.
Remove that part of the video.
note: “Cut out” means remove. “Move it to the beginning” keeps the scene and changes its place.

picture.alt: A clapperboard beside a film reel.

question: “There’s music in the background while you’re speaking.” Where is the music in this clip?
choices: You can hear it behind the speaker’s voice.
You hear it before the speaker appears.
The speaker is explaining how to play it.
It starts when the speaker has finished.
note: A background sound happens alongside the main sound. Music that plays before anyone speaks could be the introduction.

picture.alt: A vintage microphone on a stand.

question: Your partner asks for a close-up of the painting. Which shot should you take?
choices: A shot of the artist arriving at the building.
A shot from near enough to show the brush marks.
A shot of everyone standing in the gallery.
A shot of the whole wall from the doorway.
note: A close-up fills the picture with a detail. A wide shot from the doorway would help viewers see where the painting hangs.

picture.alt: A camera beside a blank photograph.

question: After your walking vlog, a classmate asks, “What stood out for you?” What does she want to hear?
choices: The time you set off on foot.
The things you left out of the vlog.
The thing you noticed most.
The place you stood to film.
note: Something stands out when it catches your attention. “What did you leave out?” asks about material the viewers never saw.

question: You’re making a video for new students taking the ferry for the first time. You’re holding a travel card at the entrance. What do you say as you show it?
choices: This card was the first thing I bought when I moved here.
This is my travel card. I use it every day to get to class.
The card saves me carrying cash when I take the ferry.
Tap your card here and wait for the green light.
note: Tapping the card gives a first-time passenger an action to copy. The story about buying yours could work in a personal vlog about your first week.

picture.alt: A ferry beside an İstanbul skyline.

question: A viewer comments, “I can see the simit. What’s it like to eat?” You’ve just taken a bite. What do you say?
choices: It’s crunchy outside and still warm inside.
It’s round, with seeds all over the top.
It cost less than the cheese sandwich next to it.
Lots of students buy one on their way to class.
note: “Crunchy” and “warm” describe what the camera can’t show. The shape and seeds would help someone recognise simit in the shop.

question: A classmate filmed an artist mixing blue and yellow paint. “Which part should I slow down so viewers can see the colour change?” she asks.
choices: The moment you say goodbye to the artist.
The moment the yellow first touches the blue.
The bit where she chooses the two tubes of paint.
The shot of the finished picture on the wall.
note: The mixing is where the change happens. Holding the final shot longer would help viewers study the finished picture.

question: In your partner’s video, a passing bus covers the name of the street. She can record just one sentence again. What feedback would help her most?
choices: Your voice sounds fine once the bus has gone.
I liked the sound of the bus. It made me feel I was there.
Could you say the street name again? The bus was loud.
Could you turn the bus sound down in that part?
note: The street name tells her exactly which line to record. Turning the bus sound down would be worth trying if her voice were still audible underneath it. Here she can record the missing name.

picture.alt: A red London bus beside a streetlamp.

question: In your café vlog you said a cup of coffee was “worth the wait.” A viewer asks what made it worth waiting for. What do you reply?
choices: We waited in the queue for about fifteen minutes.
If you want a shorter queue, try going early.
It took longer than I expected for such a small cup.
It tasted of cardamom. I’d never had coffee like that before.
note: The taste explains why the wait felt worthwhile. “Fifteen minutes” would answer “How long did you wait?”

picture.alt: A cup of Turkish coffee on a saucer.

question: Your recipe video jumps from noodles in a pot to noodles in a bowl. You used a strainer, but cut that shot. A viewer asks, “Did you pour the water into the bowl too?” What do you say?
choices: I drained the noodles first, then put them in the bowl.
I use a little of the water when the noodles look dry.
I like to leave the noodles in the pot until everyone’s ready.
Let me show you what the noodles look like in the bowl.
note: The two actions explain the missing step. Showing the bowl would reveal the result, but explaining the missing step tells the viewer how you got there.

question: You’re filming a music student who learnt a song from her grandfather. She’s ready to play it. You’d like viewers to hear how she learnt it, in her own words. What do you say?
choices: Could you tell us which other songs you’d like to learn?
Before you play, how did he teach you the song?
That sounds wonderful. Can you play the whole song twice?
I think I know how you learnt it. Shall I tell the story?
note: “How did he teach you the song?” hands the story to the person who remembers it. Asking her to play would fit once she’s told that story.

question: Your partner says, “I want to describe the walk in my vlog, but all I’ve got is ‘It was nice.’” You heard birds all along the path. What do you suggest?
choices: Could you explain why you wanted to take this walk?
How about starting with the date and time of our walk?
What about the sound of the birds on the path?
Could you say “very nice” to make it sound stronger?
note: A sound gives listeners a detail they can imagine. A date could place the walk in time without telling them what it felt like.

question: “So the bridge in your video is closed all week?” asks a viewer. People can cross on foot every day. Only cars have to wait until Monday. What do you reply?
choices: Could you come back on Monday when the work is finished?
It’s a lovely walk, especially when the sun comes out.
They’re doing some work on it until the start of next week.
You can walk across today. It’s the cars that have to wait.
note: The viewer can now tell who can cross. Mentioning the work may explain the closure but leaves the question about walking open.

picture.alt: A stone bridge over a river.

question: You and a partner are presenting a market vlog. You’ve shown the entrance. She has just interviewed a baker inside. How do you bring her into the video?
choices: That’s the way in. Elif, what did the baker show you?
That’s the way in. Elif and I both hope you enjoyed it.
Thanks, Elif. I’ll tell everyone what your baker said.
Elif, shall we show everyone the entrance once more?
note: Calling her by name and asking about the interview gives her a clear turn. “We hope you enjoyed it” sounds like the end of the video.

picture.alt: A camera beside a blank photograph.
